# Book I, Proposition 1

*An equilateral triangle on a given straight line*

> On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/01-idea.svg" alt="Each side of the triangle is a radius of the circle in its colour (blue, red), and the base, drawn in both colours, is a radius of both. So all three sides are equal." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Each side of the triangle is a radius of the circle in its colour (blue, red), and the base, drawn in both colours, is a radius of both. So all three sides are equal.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/01.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.1, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB be the given finite straight line.

Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB.

With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; [Post. 3]

again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; [Post. 3]

and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the straight lines CA, CB be joined. [Post. 1]

Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,

AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]

Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,

BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]

But CA was also proved equal to AB;

therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.

And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]

therefore CA is also equal to CB.

Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.

Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite straight line AB.

(Being) what it was required to do.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop01.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop01.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- What Euclid sees in the figure but never says: the point C, being as far
from A and from B as they are from each other, is not on the straight line
AB. So ABC really is a triangle. -/
theorem Prop1.figure {A B C : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖)
    (hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖) : Triangle A B C := by
  rintro ⟨L, hA, hB, hC⟩
  have hne : ‖A B‖ ≠ 0 := len_ne_zero hAB
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm A C).trans hCA
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm B C).trans hCB
  have hCA' : C ≠ A := fun h => hne (by rw [← hCA, h, len_self])
  have hCB' : C ≠ B := fun h => hne (by rw [← hCB, h, len_self])
  /- On one straight line, one of the three points would lie between the other two,
     and then a length would equal itself taken twice. -/
  rcases between_cases hAB hCB'.symm hCA'.symm hA hB hC with h | h | h
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [hBC, hAC] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [len_symm B A, hAC, hBC] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this
  · have := len_add_of_between h
    rw [hAC, hCB] at this
    exact Magnitude.add_self_ne hne this

/-- On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle. -/
theorem Prop1 (A B : Point) (hAB : A ≠ B) (P : Point) :
    ∃ C : Point, Equilateral A B C ∧ (¬ Collinear A B P → SameSideOf C P A B) := by
  -- Let AB be the given finite straight line.
  -- Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB.
  -- With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨BCD, hA_BCD, hB_BCD⟩ := Postulate3 A B hAB
  -- again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨ACE, hB_ACE, hA_ACE⟩ := Postulate3 B A hAB.symm
  -- and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the
  -- straight lines CA, CB be joined. [Post. 1]
  /- Euclid never says why the circles cut one another. Each passes through the
     other's centre, and a centre lies inside its circle, so they must cross
     (System E, Intersection 5). They cross on both sides of AB, so C may
     be taken on whichever side we please: on P's side, when P is off AB
     (System E, Intersections 8). Lean needs only the point C; the straight
     lines CA, CB are drawn for the eye. -/
  have hmeet := circles_meet hB_BCD (centre_inside hA_BCD) (centre_inside hB_ACE) hA_ACE
  obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hside⟩ : ∃ C : Point, OnCircle C BCD ∧ OnCircle C ACE ∧
      (¬ Collinear A B P → SameSideOf C P A B) := by
    by_cases hP : Collinear A B P
    · obtain ⟨C, -, -, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, -⟩ := hmeet
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun h => absurd hP h⟩
    · obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
      obtain ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, hCP⟩ :=
        circles_meet_same_side hmeet hA_BCD hB_ACE hA_AB hB_AB (Triangle.off_line hP hA_AB hB_AB)
      exact ⟨C, hC_BCD, hC_ACE, fun _ => SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB hCP⟩
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB,
  -- AC is equal to AB. [Def. 15]
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := Definition15 hA_BCD hC_BCD hB_BCD
  -- Again, since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE,
  -- BC is equal to BA. [Def. 15]
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖B A‖ := Definition15 hB_ACE hC_ACE hA_ACE
  -- But CA was also proved equal to AB;
  have hCA : ‖C A‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C A).trans hAC
  -- therefore each of the straight lines CA, CB is equal to AB.
  have hCB : ‖C B‖ = ‖A B‖ := (len_symm C B).trans (hBC.trans (len_symm B A))
  -- And things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; [C.N. 1]
  -- therefore CA is also equal to CB.
  have hCA_CB : ‖C A‖ = ‖C B‖ := CommonNotion1 hCA hCB
  -- Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, BC are equal to one another.
  have hAB_BC : ‖A B‖ = ‖B C‖ := (hBC.trans (len_symm B A)).symm
  have hBC_CA : ‖B C‖ = ‖C A‖ := (len_symm B C).trans (hCA_CB.symm)
  -- Therefore the triangle ABC is equilateral; and it has been constructed on the given finite
  -- straight line AB.
  exact ⟨C, ⟨Prop1.figure hAB hCA hCB, hAB_BC, hBC_CA⟩, hside⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.
```

_Postulates, definitions, Common Notions and tacit rules: all that this proof rests on, counting those of the propositions it cites._

<details><summary>The 15 tacit rules beneath this proof</summary>

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

**Must the circles meet?** Euclid's very first step uses something none of his postulates says: that the two circles cut one another. Heath puts it plainly: "It is a commonplace that Euclid has no right to assume, without premising some postulate, that the two circles *will* meet in a point C" (vol. 1, p. 242). We supply it as a named rule, [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean), from System E, a modern list of the facts Euclid reads off his figures (its Intersection 5): if each circle passes through a point inside the other, they cross. Here each passes through the other's centre.

**Could AC and BC run together?** Heath recalls Zeno's remark "that the problem is not solved unless it is taken for granted that two straight lines cannot have a common segment" (vol. 1, p. 242): AC and BC might meet short of C and run on together, spoiling the triangle. Postulate 2 settles that, Heath answers, and our proof never meets the worry, for it needs only the point C, not the straight lines CA and CB that Euclid joins. Zeno's other doubt, that the two circumferences might have a common part, waits for III.10; meanwhile "it is enough for the purpose of this proposition if *one* equilateral triangle can be found with the given base" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 243).

**Is ABC a triangle, and on which side?** Euclid never says that C is off the straight line AB, though only that makes ABC a triangle. Lean wants it said, so `Prop1.figure` proves it: if C were on AB, one of the three points would lie between the other two, and some length would equal itself taken twice, which Common Notion 5, the whole greater than the part, forbids. The circles cross on both sides of AB, and I.9 and I.11 need a particular side, so our I.1 lets the side be named. That means naming the straight line AB, by Postulate 1, and calling on the rule that the circles cross on each side of it (System E, Intersections 8).

**The modern way.** Put A at 0 and B at 1 in the complex plane, and C is 1/2 + (√3/2)i, the point reached by turning AB through 60°. That √3 tells the whole story: in the plane of points with rational coordinates all five of Euclid's postulates hold, yet the two circles of I.1 slip past each other without meeting, as Robin Hartshorne's *Geometry: Euclid and Beyond* explains beautifully. So the tacit rule is doing real work: it says the plane has the square roots that ruler and compass need.

## Further reading

- For turning AB through 60° with one multiplication, Tristan Needham's [*Visual Complex Analysis*](https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780192868916.001.0001) (2023), ch. 1, "Geometry and Complex Arithmetic", a book that explains complex numbers almost entirely in pictures.
- For the plane of rational points, where the two circles of I.1 slip past each other, Robin Hartshorne's [*Geometry: Euclid and Beyond*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-22676-7) (2000), the book the modern way above draws on, written to be read alongside the *Elements*.
- For Euclid in colour, Nicholas Rougeux's [*Byrne's Euclid*](https://www.c82.net/euclid/) (2018, free online), Oliver Byrne's edition of 1847, whose colours our "at a glance" figures borrow, rebuilt for the web with interactive figures.
